description: This is a team comprised of members of the high browncil, ardent space and walking enthusiasts.
summary:
Choosing a landing site near the Moon’s south pole is challenging because of its uneven terrain, limited sunlight, and difficulties maintaining direct communication with Earth. Our project, Lunar South Pole Mission Planner, is an interactive website designed to help mission planners, researchers, and the public explore and compare potential landing sites for future Artemis missions.

Using real NASA lunar terrain data and SPICE ephemerides, we calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to different landing sites, accounting for obstructions from the surrounding terrain. Users can explore an interactive lunar map, move through time, view the surface from different locations, and analyse sunlight and Earth visibility over time. The website also allows users to compare landing sites and dates against mission requirements, such as illumination, communication availability, and terrain slope, to identify suitable landing opportunities.

By bringing these datasets and calculations together in an accessible interface, our project helps users better understand the challenges and trade-offs involved in planning missions to the lunar south pole.
details:
Our Idea

Our starting idea was simple: what if we could build something like Google Earth and Street View, but for the Moon?

With NASA’s Artemis programme preparing for future missions to the lunar south pole, we wanted to create a way for anyone to explore potential landing sites and understand the challenges involved in choosing one.

Unlike most places on Earth, the lunar south pole has unusual lighting conditions. The Sun remains close to the horizon, meaning even small hills can block sunlight for extended periods. Earth also moves in and out of view, making direct communication difficult. Furthermore, delays in a mission’s landing date can significantly change the conditions a spacecraft encounters.

We wanted to go beyond simply displaying lunar imagery. Our aim was to build an interactive tool that combines realistic surface visualisation with the scientific calculations needed to compare landing sites and make informed mission-planning decisions.

What We Developed

We developed Lunar South Pole Mission Planner, an interactive website that allows users to explore the lunar south pole, investigate potential landing locations, and compare their suitability for future missions.

The website has four main components:

  • Interactive lunar map: Users can explore a 3D lunar globe using NASA imagery, select between four study locations, and view information about their terrain, sunlight availability, and Earth visibility. A one-minute guided tour introduces the main features for users unfamiliar with lunar exploration.
  • Lunar Street View: Users can explore the lunar surface from different viewpoints, with terrain horizons calculated using real lunar elevation data. The Sun and Earth are positioned accurately in the sky, allowing users to see how surrounding mountains and craters obstruct their view. Users can also walk between approximately nine viewpoints extending up to 1.5 km from a landing site, each with its own terrain horizon and visibility calculations. This allows users to investigate how even small changes in location affect sunlight and communication conditions.
  • Visibility and landing-delay analysis: Our tool calculates when the Sun and Earth are visible from each location, accounting for surrounding terrain and eclipses. Users can explore 30-day visibility timelines, identify periods of continuous sunlight or communication availability, and investigate how delaying a landing by 3, 7, 14 or 30 days changes these conditions. The tool also identifies suitable locations for different landing dates.
  • Mission planner and site comparison: Users can compare up to three landing scenarios against mission requirements, including sunlight availability, communication blackouts, terrain slope, and conditions at touchdown. The tool also estimates sunlight energy reaching a solar panel and checks battery requirements against the longest period of darkness. It then recommends suitable scenarios based on the selected constraints and explains why others may be less suitable.

Together, these features allow users to move from exploring the lunar surface to evaluating the practical challenges of operating there.

How It Works

Our project combines NASA datasets with physics-based calculations to produce the information displayed on the website.

1. Lunar Terrain Modelling

We use elevation data from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), including high-resolution 5 m terrain maps around selected sites and an 80 m regional map.

From these datasets, we calculate a 360° terrain horizon around each location by tracing rays across the lunar surface, extending up to 160 km and accounting for the Moon’s curvature. Five rays are traced per degree of azimuth to sample terrain obstructions more thoroughly.

This allows us to determine which parts of the sky are obstructed by nearby and distant terrain.

We also calculate horizons for observer heights of 2 m, 5 m and 10 m, allowing users to investigate how placing equipment on an elevated structure could improve visibility.

2. Sun and Earth Positioning

We use NASA/JPL’s SPICE toolkit with DE440 planetary ephemerides and lunar orientation data to calculate the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth as seen from each site.

These calculations account for light-travel time and aberration, providing the positions an observer would actually see from the lunar surface.

We independently checked these calculations against JPL Horizons, achieving agreement better than 0.00001° for the tested locations and dates.

3. Visibility and Mission Analysis

By combining the Sun and Earth positions with the calculated terrain horizons, we determine when each body is visible and identify continuous visibility and blackout periods.

The calculations also account for the Earth obstructing the Sun during lunar eclipses.

Users can adjust visibility requirements, such as whether the Sun’s upper edge, centre, or entire disc must be visible, or whether Earth must clear the terrain by an additional margin.

These results feed into our mission planner, which evaluates landing scenarios against user-defined operational constraints, including illumination, communication availability, terrain slope, and landing delays.

Importantly, the mission planner evaluates these conditions from the moment of touchdown, allowing users to understand how much sunlight and communication availability remain after landing.

4. Interactive Visualisation and Software

We developed the scientific calculations in Python, using libraries including SpiceyPy, NumPy and SciPy. Terrain processing also uses Rasterio and PyProj.

A FastAPI backend connects the terrain and science calculations to the website, while the frontend was developed using React, TypeScript, Three.js and Vite, with the application deployed through Vercel and Render.

This allows users to interact with the scientific results through a 3D lunar globe, surface-level visualisations, interactive timelines, graphs, and landing-site comparisons, without needing to understand or run the underlying code.

The website also includes a guided tour, mobile-friendly layouts and accessibility features to make the information easier to explore.

What Makes Our Project Different?

The main idea behind our project is to connect lunar exploration with practical mission planning in one accessible platform.

NASA already provides extensive lunar imagery, elevation data, and scientific tools. However, using these resources to investigate a specific landing site often requires specialised software and technical knowledge.

We wanted to bring these capabilities together in a way that anyone could understand and use.

Our Lunar Street View was a particularly important part of this idea. Rather than looking at a top-down map and trying to imagine the surrounding terrain, users can explore the surface and directly see why the Sun or Earth might be blocked.

More importantly, the surface view is connected to the same scientific calculations used by the mission planner. This means users can investigate how moving a few metres, changing their observer height, or delaying a landing affects the suitability of a location.

Several examples from our analysis demonstrate this:

  • Shackleton Rim: Our model predicts that moving just 54 m from a published study point to a nearby elevated location increases sunlight availability over a 30-day period from 0% to 98%, while Earth visibility increases from 0% to 59%. This demonstrates how even small differences in local terrain can significantly affect landing-site suitability.
  • Connecting Ridge: Delaying a landing by seven days reduces the time before the first sunset from 8.3 days to just 31 hours. This demonstrates why landing dates and potential mission delays must be considered alongside the choice of location.
  • Exploring the surface: Moving approximately 400 m southwest of Connecting Ridge reduces predicted sunlight availability from 81% to 37%, and Earth visibility from 44% to 11%. This shows how our Street View can be used to investigate real differences in local conditions rather than simply visualising the terrain.

These examples show how our tool can reveal engineering trade-offs that may not be immediately apparent from lunar maps alone.

Impact and Applications

Our project is designed for three main audiences:

  • Mission planners and researchers: As a preliminary analysis tool for exploring potential landing sites, comparing operational conditions, and identifying locations or periods worth investigating further.
  • Students and educators: As an interactive way to understand lunar geography, orbital geometry, illumination, and the engineering challenges of operating near the lunar poles.
  • The general public: As an accessible way to explore the Moon and understand the scientific and engineering decisions behind future Artemis missions.

The wider aim is to make NASA’s scientific data more accessible and useful. Rather than simply presenting information, our website allows users to interact with it, ask questions, and investigate different scenarios themselves.

We also see potential for the platform to be extended to other lunar regions, additional mission requirements, and future surface exploration activities.

Scientific Considerations and Limitations

Throughout development, we focused on keeping the calculations grounded in real scientific data while making the website accessible to non-specialists.

Some of our main considerations included:

  • Scientific accuracy: Using established NASA datasets and SPICE ephemerides, with independent validation of the Sun and Earth positioning calculations.
  • Terrain resolution: Accounting for the fact that small changes in location can significantly affect visibility, particularly near the lunar poles.
  • Mission timing: Considering how landing delays affect sunlight availability and communication opportunities, rather than evaluating locations under fixed conditions.
  • Different mission requirements: Allowing users to adjust constraints rather than assuming that one landing site is suitable for every mission.
  • Accessibility: Presenting complex calculations through intuitive visualisations, a guided tour, and explanations of the underlying science.
  • Transparency: Clearly explaining our assumptions, data sources, and limitations within the website.

Our terrain horizons are derived from real NASA elevation data, although they have not yet been independently validated against observed lunar illumination conditions.

Our model also evaluates individual locations rather than complete landing areas. This is particularly important because NASA’s published Artemis III landing requirements include landing within 100 m of a target, while our results demonstrate that illumination conditions can change significantly over much shorter distances. Similarly, our terrain slope estimates are based on individual 5 m DEM cells rather than a complete landing-zone assessment.

The tool also does not model every aspect of a lunar mission, such as thermal conditions, detailed electrical power generation, or communication link budgets. Earth visibility represents a direct line of sight rather than a guaranteed communication link, while the sunlight calculations do not guarantee sufficient electrical power.

For these reasons, we present the website as an exploratory mission-planning tool rather than a replacement for detailed engineering analysis.

Our Goal

Ultimately, we wanted to make exploring and understanding the lunar south pole as intuitive as exploring a location on Earth.

What began as an idea for a Google Earth and Street View experience for the Moon developed into a tool that also helps users understand where, when, and why a lunar landing might be feasible.

By combining NASA’s scientific data with interactive visualisation and mission-planning capabilities, we hope to make lunar exploration more accessible while demonstrating how these datasets can support real engineering decisions.
